body:
Meaning of Revolutionary Nationalism

Revolutionary nationalism was a stream of the Indian freedom struggle in which organised groups sought to overthrow British colonial rule through revolutionary action, including armed resistance. Its supporters believed that petitions, constitutional demands and peaceful protests alone would not compel the British government to surrender political power.

Revolutionary nationalists formed secret societies, recruited young activists, circulated political literature and organised actions against symbols of colonial authority. Their principal political objective was Indian independence. However, their ideas about the society that should emerge after independence differed. Some early groups concentrated mainly on ending foreign rule, while later organisations such as the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association also advocated a society without economic exploitation.

Revolutionary nationalism: A form of anti-colonial nationalism that sought political independence through revolutionary organisation and action rather than relying exclusively on constitutional methods or non-violent mass protest.

Why Did Revolutionary Organisations Emerge?

Disappointment with Constitutional Methods

During the early Indian national movement, moderate leaders generally used petitions, resolutions and constitutional demands to obtain political reforms. A section of younger nationalists considered these methods too slow and ineffective against colonial domination.

Partition of Bengal and the Swadeshi Movement

The British government partitioned Bengal in 1905. The decision generated strong nationalist opposition. The Swadeshi movement encouraged the boycott of foreign goods, the use of Indian products and the establishment of national educational institutions.

Some young nationalists believed that the movement needed more forceful action. Secret revolutionary organisations consequently expanded in Bengal. Anushilan Samiti and the circle associated with Jugantar became important centres of this activity.

Withdrawal of the Non-Cooperation Movement

Another important phase began after 1922. Mahatma Gandhi withdrew the Non-Cooperation Movement following the violent incident at Chauri Chaura, where a police station was attacked and policemen were killed. Gandhi insisted that a movement based on non-violence could not continue through such methods.

Some young nationalists were disappointed by the withdrawal. They believed that a more direct revolutionary struggle was necessary. This atmosphere contributed to the reorganisation of revolutionary groups in northern India, including the establishment of the Hindustan Republican Association in 1924.

Influence of Socialist Ideas

The Russian Revolution of 1917 encouraged interest in socialism among sections of India's educated youth. Socialist ideas emphasised the position of workers and peasants and criticised economic exploitation.

These ideas became particularly important to Bhagat Singh and other revolutionaries who reorganised the Hindustan Republican Association as the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association in 1928.

Revolutionary Action and Gandhian Mass Movements

Revolutionary nationalism and Gandhian nationalism opposed the same colonial government, but their methods differed. Gandhi made non-violence a fundamental principle of political struggle and organised large public campaigns. Revolutionary organisations accepted the use of armed action against colonial authority.

Both approaches existed within the broader Indian national movement. Individual revolutionaries sometimes participated in non-violent campaigns before adopting revolutionary methods. Participation in one stream therefore did not necessarily mean complete separation from the other.

Principal Centres of Revolutionary Activity

  • Bengal: Anushilan Samiti, Jugantar and later the Chittagong revolutionary group.
  • United Provinces: The Hindustan Republican Association and the Kakori action near Lucknow.
  • Punjab and Delhi: The Hindustan Socialist Republican Association and activities associated with Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Chandrashekhar Azad.
  • Chittagong: The Indian Republican Army, Chittagong Branch, led by Surya Sen. Chittagong was then part of British India and is now in Bangladesh.

The colonial government responded to revolutionary activity through surveillance, restrictions on publications, arrests, conspiracy trials, imprisonment and executions. These responses became important events in the development of the revolutionary movement itself.

Prelims focus

  • The Partition of Bengal in 1905 encouraged the growth of revolutionary organisations in Bengal.
  • The withdrawal of the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1922 contributed to renewed revolutionary activity.
  • The Hindustan Republican Association was established in 1924.
  • The Hindustan Socialist Republican Association emerged from the reorganisation of the HRA in 1928.
  • Surya Sen led the Chittagong revolutionary movement associated with the armoury raid of 1930.
  • Trap: Revolutionary nationalism and Gandhian non-violent nationalism shared the objective of ending colonial rule but differed in their accepted methods.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts-III, Class 8, chapter The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947, printed pp. 113–120; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World-II, Class 10, chapter Nationalism in India, section on revolutionary nationalism, printed p. 65; Indira Gandhi National Open University, History of India VIII (c. 1857–1950), Unit 9, The Revolutionaries, sections 9.1, 9.2 and 9.6, printed pp. 116–118 and 123–125, consulted 21 November 2026.]

title: Revolutionary Nationalism: Meaning, Causes and Development

body:
Anushilan Samiti: Origins and Organisation

Anushilan Samiti was an influential revolutionary organisation that developed in Calcutta, now Kolkata, during the early years of the 20th century. Its beginnings are generally dated to 1902.

The early organisation brought together nationalist youth who were interested in physical training, personal discipline, political education and resistance to British rule. Physical-culture associations and study circles provided important meeting places for revolutionary-minded students.

Pramathanath Mitra and Satish Chandra Basu were important figures in its early development. Jatindranath Banerjee and Barindra Kumar Ghosh were also associated with the revolutionary circles from which the organisation grew. Aurobindo Ghosh was connected with the wider network of militant nationalists in Bengal.

Historical accounts differ in identifying a single founder because the early organisation developed through several closely connected circles. It is therefore more accurate to distinguish its early organisers from the leaders of its later branches.

Dhaka Anushilan Samiti

A major revolutionary organisation developed in Dhaka in 1906 under the leadership of Pulin Behari Das. It became known as the Dhaka or Dacca Anushilan Samiti.

The Dhaka organisation expanded revolutionary activity in eastern Bengal. Its leadership and geographical centre should not be confused with those of the earlier Calcutta organisation.

Calcutta Anushilan: Early development around 1902; associated with Pramathanath Mitra and other organisers.
Dhaka Anushilan: Established in 1906 under Pulin Behari Das.

Jugantar: Newspaper and Revolutionary Group

Jugantar, also written Yugantar, means a new age or change of era. The name became associated with a Bengali revolutionary weekly newspaper launched in 1906 and with the revolutionary circle connected to that publication.

Barindra Kumar Ghosh, the younger brother of Aurobindo Ghosh, played a leading role in the circle. Bhupendranath Datta was another important associate of the newspaper. The publication encouraged resistance to colonial rule and helped spread revolutionary nationalist ideas.

The Jugantar group emerged from revolutionary networks that overlapped with Calcutta Anushilan. The 2 names therefore refer to closely connected developments, but they should not be treated as interchangeable names for every branch or member of the revolutionary movement in Bengal.

The Muzaffarpur Incident of 1908

One major revolutionary episode occurred at Muzaffarpur in Bihar on 30 April 1908.

Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki, associated with the Bengal revolutionary movement, attempted to kill the British judicial officer Douglas Kingsford, who was regarded by the revolutionaries as particularly harsh towards nationalist activists.

The attack failed to kill Kingsford. Instead, a bomb struck another carriage, killing 2 English women. This distinction is important: the intended target survived, while people who were not the intended targets lost their lives.

Prafulla Chaki died by suicide while attempting to avoid arrest. Khudiram Bose was arrested, tried and executed on 11 August 1908.

The Alipore Bomb Case

The investigation following the Muzaffarpur incident led the colonial authorities to the revolutionary network operating from Maniktala in Calcutta.

Several revolutionaries, including Aurobindo Ghosh and Barindra Kumar Ghosh, were arrested and prosecuted in the Alipore Bomb Case of 1908–1909.

Aurobindo Ghosh was acquitted. Barindra Kumar Ghosh and Ullaskar Dutt received death sentences that were subsequently commuted to transportation for life.

The case seriously affected the organisation of revolutionary activity in Bengal. The British government also strengthened restrictions on nationalist publications, including through the Newspapers (Incitement to Offences) Act, 1908, which permitted action against publications considered to encourage offences.

Important Distinctions

OrganisationBeginning and centrePrincipal associations
Calcutta Anushilan SamitiAround 1902, CalcuttaPramathanath Mitra, Satish Chandra Basu and other early organisers
Dhaka Anushilan Samiti1906, DhakaPulin Behari Das
Jugantar1906, BengalRevolutionary weekly and associated group; Barindra Kumar Ghosh and Bhupendranath Datta

Prelims focus

  • Anushilan Samiti developed in Calcutta around 1902.
  • Pulin Behari Das led the Dhaka Anushilan Samiti established in 1906.
  • Jugantar began as a Bengali revolutionary weekly in 1906 and became associated with a revolutionary group.
  • Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki were associated with the Muzaffarpur incident of 30 April 1908.
  • Aurobindo Ghosh was acquitted in the Alipore Bomb Case.
  • Trap: Khudiram Bose was executed, but Douglas Kingsford, the intended target at Muzaffarpur, survived.

[Sources: Government of Tamil Nadu, SCERT, Higher Secondary Second Year History, Vol. 1, 2019, Unit 2, Rise of Extremism and Swadeshi Movement, printed pp. 22–24; Ministry of Education, Press Information Bureau, Shri Dharmendra Pradhan calls for including information about Anusilan Samity in NCF, 24 July 2022, consulted 21 November 2026; Government of West Bengal, West Bengal Police, historical account of the Intelligence Branch, consulted 21 November 2026; Publications Division, Government of India, Yojana, August 2024, account of the Muzaffarpur incident, consulted 21 November 2026.]

body:
Formation of the Hindustan Republican Association

The Hindustan Republican Association (HRA) was established in 1924 as an important revolutionary organisation in northern India.

Its principal organisers included Sachindranath Sanyal, Jogesh Chandra Chatterjee and Ram Prasad Bismil. A significant organisational meeting took place at Kanpur in October 1924.

The HRA aimed to overthrow British colonial rule and establish a republic in India. Its programme envisaged a federal republic with political representation based on adult franchise, meaning that voting rights would be available to adults rather than restricted to a privileged minority.

The organisation attracted young revolutionaries who had become dissatisfied with the continuation of colonial rule, particularly after the withdrawal of the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1922.

Important Members

  • Ram Prasad Bismil: An important organiser and leading figure in the Kakori action.
  • Ashfaqullah Khan: A close associate of Bismil and participant in the Kakori action.
  • Rajendra Nath Lahiri: A revolutionary associated with the organisation and the Kakori action.
  • Chandrashekhar Azad: A revolutionary who participated in the Kakori action and later helped reorganise the movement.
  • Sachindranath Sanyal and Jogesh Chandra Chatterjee: Important figures in the establishment and organisation of the HRA.

The Kakori Train Action: 9 August 1925

The Kakori train action took place on 9 August 1925 near Kakori, close to Lucknow in the United Provinces, now Uttar Pradesh.

Members of the HRA stopped a train travelling towards Lucknow and seized money being transported for the British government treasury. Their purpose was to obtain funds for the revolutionary organisation and challenge colonial authority.

Ram Prasad Bismil, Ashfaqullah Khan, Rajendra Nath Lahiri and Chandrashekhar Azad were among the revolutionaries associated with the action.

The incident also caused the death of a passenger who was not an intended target. Although the HRA members sought government funds rather than private passengers' possessions, this death became an important part of the criminal prosecution.

Organisation: Hindustan Republican Association.
Event: Kakori train action.
Date: 9 August 1925.
Place: Near Kakori, Lucknow, United Provinces.
Immediate objective: Seizure of government treasury money to support revolutionary activities.

British Response: The Kakori Conspiracy Case

The colonial government launched extensive investigations and arrested numerous revolutionaries associated with the HRA.

The accused were prosecuted in the Kakori Conspiracy Case. The trial resulted in severe punishments, including death sentences, transportation for life and long periods of imprisonment.

4 revolutionaries were executed in December 1927 in connection with the case.

RevolutionaryExecution dateConnection
Rajendra Nath Lahiri17 December 1927HRA revolutionary and Kakori participant
Ram Prasad Bismil19 December 1927HRA organiser and Kakori leader
Ashfaqullah Khan19 December 1927HRA revolutionary and Kakori participant
Thakur Roshan Singh19 December 1927HRA associate sentenced in the broader Kakori conspiracy prosecution

The list of people executed in the Kakori case should not be confused with the list of people physically present during the train action. The prosecution covered a wider revolutionary conspiracy.

Chandrashekhar Azad escaped arrest following the Kakori action and continued revolutionary activities.

Consequences for the Revolutionary Movement

The executions and imprisonment of HRA members weakened its original leadership. However, revolutionary activity did not end.

Surviving revolutionaries, including Chandrashekhar Azad, worked with a younger generation that included Bhagat Singh and Sukhdev. In 1928, the HRA was reorganised as the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA).

The addition of Socialist to its name reflected the growing importance of social and economic equality in the organisation's political objectives.

Prelims focus

  • The HRA was established in 1924, with an important organisational meeting at Kanpur.
  • Sachindranath Sanyal, Jogesh Chandra Chatterjee and Ram Prasad Bismil were important HRA organisers.
  • The Kakori train action took place on 9 August 1925 near Lucknow.
  • Rajendra Nath Lahiri was executed on 17 December 1927.
  • Bismil, Ashfaqullah Khan and Roshan Singh were executed on 19 December 1927.
  • Trap: Kakori was an HRA action in 1925, not an HSRA action in 1928.

[Sources: Indira Gandhi National Open University, History of India VIII (c. 1857–1950), Unit 9, sections 9.6–9.7, printed pp. 124–125, consulted 21 November 2026; Ministry of Culture, Government of India, Dictionary of Martyrs: India's Freedom Struggle (1857–1947), Vol. 2, Part I and Part II, entries on Chandrashekhar Azad, Rajendra Nath Lahiri and Roshan Singh, consulted 21 November 2026; Government of India, New India Samachar, 1–15 August 2025, p. 2, Kakori Train Incident, consulted 21 November 2026; The Indian Express, 19 December 2023, account of the Kakori executions, consulted 21 November 2026.]
